prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth map supports a coarse layered layout: in frame 1, several people occupy the near left and centre at roughly 0.5–2 m, while the floor and street extend farther behind them; in frames 2–5, the wooden counter is nearest at about 0.3–1 m, with the person behind it around 1–2 m and the rear wall and shelves farther away. Across frames 2–5, the counter sweeps from centre-left toward the lower-right as the camera wearer turns and moves alongside it, while the person behind the counter remains ahead and shifts horizontally in the view rather than clearly approaching or retreating. Bright counter surfaces and nearby bodies make arm’s-reach regions easier to distinguish than in RGB, and the map also exposes large foreground occlusions caused by the counter. Metric distances remain highly uncertain because this is monocular depth: surfaces are smoothed into broad planes, jars and small objects merge together, and repeated bright wedges and distorted person shapes suggest unreliable geometry near boundaries and across frames.
descriptions.segmentation: The segmentation map isolates multiple people in frame 1, including several partly cut off at the left, top, and centre-right edges, and shows overlapping masks where one body occludes another; these people are roughly 0.5–2 m from the camera and close enough to one another that some are separated by less than about a metre. In frames 2–5 it consistently marks the person behind the counter about 1–2 m ahead, shifting from left-of-centre to right-of-centre as the camera turns, while a small bottle appears high near the centre in frame 3 and a chair appears to the right of the person in frame 4. The map clarifies instance boundaries and class identity where RGB textures are cluttered, but it provides little direct depth, facing direction, gaze, or above/below information beyond the masks’ image positions. It is unreliable for full layout because the counter, shelves, jars, display case, and most small objects are unlabelled, several people are fragmented or missed, and truncated masks at image edges do not reveal how far bodies continue outside the view.
descriptions.pose: The pose map gives the clearest body geometry in frame 1: a near person left-of-centre has a visible upper-body skeleton roughly 0.5–1.5 m away, with head above torso and arms extending downward, while nearby people and hands are mostly absent or only represented by isolated keypoints. In frames 3–4, sparse skeletons mark the person behind the counter about 1–2 m ahead and a smaller arm/hand configuration lower and to the right, helping localize limbs relative to the counter even when clothing and background overlap in RGB. The detected torso orientation suggests the near frame-1 person is angled partly toward the camera wearer and the later person is approximately front-facing or oblique, but head and eye keypoints are insufficient to determine reliable gaze. No confident skeleton appears in frames 2 or 5, limb lengths and joints are incomplete, and most hands are missing, so arm’s reach, occluded limbs, turning, and approach or retreat cannot be tracked reliably across all five frames.
